title: Go 1.5 Release Notes
why: The primary release notes documenting the Go toolchain's move from C to Go and the resulting self-hosting build requirement.

title: Installing Go from source
why: Official statement of the minimum bootstrap Go compiler for each Go version and the general bootstrap version policy.

title: What Bootstrapping does - Rust Compiler Development Guide

title: Reflections on Trusting Trust (Turing Award Lecture)
why: Thompson's own account of a compiler that reproduces a Trojan horse, the canonical source for the trust problem in bootstrapping.

claim: In Go 1.5 the compiler and runtime became written entirely in Go and assembler, so C is no longer part of the implementation and the C compiler once needed to build the distribution is gone.
quote: The compiler and runtime are now written entirely in Go (with a little assembler). C is no longer involved in the implementation, and so the C compiler that was once necessary for building the distribution is gone.

claim: The Go 1.5 compiler was produced by automatic translation of the C code into Go, deliberately kept the same program rather than being a new implementation.
quote: Most important, the compiler was actually moved by automatic translation of the C code into Go. It is in effect the same program in a different language. It is not a new implementation of the compiler so we expect the process will not have introduced new compiler bugs.

locator: Install Go compiler binaries for bootstrap
claim: The general bootstrap policy is that Go version 1.N requires a Go 1.M compiler where M is N-2 rounded down to an even number, so Go 1.24 and 1.25 require Go 1.22.
quote: Going forward, Go version 1.N will require a Go 1.M compiler, where M is N-2 rounded down to an even number. Example: Go 1.24 and 1.25 require Go 1.22.

locator: Install Go compiler binaries for bootstrap
claim: The minimum bootstrap compiler depends on the target version: a C toolchain for Go <= 1.4, a Go 1.4 compiler for 1.5 to 1.19, a Go 1.17 compiler for 1.20 to 1.21, and a Go 1.20 compiler for 1.22 to 1.23.
quote: Go <= 1.4: a C toolchain. 1.5 <= Go <= 1.19: a Go 1.4 compiler. 1.20 <= Go <= 1.21: a Go 1.17 compiler. 1.22 <= Go <= 1.23: a Go 1.20 compiler.

locator: What Bootstrapping does - Stages of bootstrapping - Overview
claim: rustc's bootstrap has stage0, the pre-compiled compiler and standard library; stage1, built from current code by an earlier compiler; and stage2, the truly current compiler.
quote:
Stage 0: the pre-compiled compiler and standard library
Stage 1: from current code, by an earlier compiler
Stage 2: the truly current compiler

claim: The stage2 compiler is produced by rebuilding the compiler with the stage1 compiler and the in-tree standard library.
quote: We then rebuild the compiler using stage1 compiler with in-tree std to produce the stage2 compiler.

claim: A modified compiler binary can be installed so that even after the Trojan-horse code is removed from its source, the binary reinserts the bugs whenever it compiles itself, leaving the login command bugged with no trace in source.
quote: We can now remove the bugs from the source of the compiler and the new binary will reinsert the bugs whenever it is compiled. Of course, the login command will remain bugged with no trace in source anywhere.

claim: Thompson's stated moral is that you cannot trust code you did not entirely create yourself, and no source-level verification or scrutiny protects you from using untrusted code.
quote: The moral is obvious. You can't trust code that you did not totally create yourself. (Especially code from companies that employ people like me.) No amount of source-level verification or scrutiny will protect you from using untrusted code.
